name: Victoria
summary_text: The Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025 (No. 11 of 2025, passed April 2025) created both civil and criminal vilification offences and extended protection beyond race and religion to disability, gender identity, sex, sex characteristics, sexual orientation and personal association (Equal Opportunity Act 2010, new Part 6A, s.102B). Victoria is the only Australian jurisdiction where public incitement against a trans person is now a criminal charge, not merely a civil complaint. The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities 2006 binds public authorities and provides an independent review mechanism absent in NSW, WA and SA. A Victorian coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women (Bridget Flack, Heather Pierard, Matt Byrne, Natalie Wilson and a fifth identified only as "AS") found Victoria Police failed the search for Flack. Coroner Ingrid Giles issued nine recommendations calling for an overhaul of missing-persons risk assessment for trans people. Advocates characterised the police handling as "a terrible miscarriage of justice." The finding documents a serious institutional failure, but the reform process and the 2025 legislation represent a corrective institutional response that counts as positive evidence under the single-incident and institutional-response rules. Academic review confirms that Victorian LGBT prison protections are policy-based and not legally enforceable, a cross-jurisdictional weakness. Vs the national score of 0.86, Victoria sits 0.02 above: the criminal vilification offence is the strongest new legal protection in the country and the Charter adds a structural review mechanism, but the coronial finding on police failure toward a specifically vulnerable sub-population (trans women in sex-work-adjacent contexts) and the thinness of prison policy prevent a larger positive deviation. Vs ACT (0.88), which also has a rights statute and self-ID custody but no equivalent criminal vilification offence and no comparable institutional-failure finding, the two units are at parity from different evidence.

sources.title: Fact sheet - explaining Victoria’s new anti-hate laws | Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission
sources.claim_summary: Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission fact sheet explaining the new anti-hate laws: the 2025 Act passed in April 2025 creates civil vilification grounds under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 (inciting hatred; hateful conduct a reasonable member of the target group would consider hateful) and criminal offences under the Crimes Act; protection extends to disability, gender identity, race, religious belief, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation (plus association), with civil grounds commencing 15 April 2026.

sources.title: Coroner calls for urgent investment into health care for trans community, following five tragic deaths - ABC News
sources.claim_summary: ABC News report (29 August 2024) on the Victorian coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women in Melbourne during the pandemic (lead case: Bridget Flack, missing December 2020, died by suicide aged 28): Coroner Ingrid Giles identified multiple Victoria Police failings and made nine recommendations, including urgent investment in trans health care and reform of missing-persons practice; the government is reviewing the recommendations.

sources.title: Coroner urges Victoria Police missing person overhaul after probe into deaths of young trans women including Bridget Flack, Natalie Wilson, Matt Byrne, Heather Pierard
sources.claim_summary: The Age report (29 August 2024, paywalled - partial text retrieved) from the Victorian Coroners Court inquest: Coroner Ingrid Giles urged an overhaul of missing-persons procedures after the probe into the deaths of young trans women, the companion framing to the ABC account of the nine recommendations.
